questions.question: How would you render API search results without creating an XSS risk?
questions.title: Safely rendering API results
questions.direct_answer: Treat API fields as untrusted data, create the required elements explicitly, and assign plain values through textContent or safe properties. If rich HTML is truly required, place sanitization and Trusted Types at one reviewed boundary rather than filtering strings by hand.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to connect DOM API choice with an end-to-end trust boundary.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming a same-origin API response is safe and assigning its fields to innerHTML.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Escaping depends on output context; URL, style, attribute, and HTML contexts do not share one universal filter.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Treat every external string as data unless a trust contract proves otherwise.
Use textContent for result labels and createElement for known structure.
Validate URLs and other typed properties before assignment.
Sanitize required rich HTML at one enforced, reviewed boundary.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
API responses are data, not trusted markup. Search results should be rendered by creating the known result structure and placing names, descriptions, and other plain fields through `textContent`.

For example, each result can become an `li` containing an anchor and description. The title is assigned as text, while the URL is parsed against an allowed base and accepted only when its protocol and destination meet the product's rule.

Sending an API field through `innerHTML` creates an injection sink. A malicious or compromised record could contain an image error handler or another HTML payload that executes in the user's origin.

When the product genuinely accepts rich text, a maintained sanitizer and an enforced Trusted Types policy or safe sanitizing API should own that boundary. Handwritten removal of script tags is not enough because HTML has many executable contexts.

The secure design keeps structure in code, text as text, and rich markup behind one explicit security control. A restrictive content security policy adds defense in depth but does not make unsafe DOM insertion correct.

sections.title: DOM injection data flow
sections.content: The useful question is not merely “did this come from our API?” but “who could influence it before it reached this DOM sink?” Stored user content, partner feeds, imported records, and compromised backend data all cross trust boundaries. The output API must match the type intended on screen.

sections.title: Different properties have different validation rules
sections.content: textContent safely represents text because the browser does not parse it as markup. A link destination is not text once assigned to `href`, so it needs URL parsing and an allowed protocol or origin rule. Event-handler properties should never be built from strings. This context-aware model scales better than trying to run every field through one generic escape function.

sections.title: Trust path for one result
sections.content:
API field
  ├─ label or description → `textContent`
  ├─ URL → parse + allow-list → `href`
  └─ required rich HTML → maintained sanitizer → TrustedHTML boundary
                                      ↓
                                DOM insertion

sections.title: Build a result without parsing its text as HTML

questions.question: How would you keep a large, frequently updated DOM list responsive?
questions.title: Responsive large DOM lists
questions.direct_answer: Measure the actual bottleneck, render only the rows the user can see when the list is very large, group related DOM work, and move expensive data preparation away from each frame. Stable keys, delegated events, and incremental updates avoid rebuilding the whole list.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of DOM size, main-thread work, measurement, and incremental rendering.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Appending thousands of nodes on every update or adding a separate handler during every render.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Virtualization adds focus, accessibility, measurement, and scroll-position complexity; small lists are often clearer without it.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Profile first to separate scripting, layout, paint, and network time.
Update changed rows instead of replacing the entire list.
Virtualize very large lists so only a visible window is mounted.
Keep per-frame work small and preserve keyboard and screen-reader behaviour.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A large live list becomes unresponsive when too much JavaScript and rendering work occupies the main thread. The solution begins with a performance trace that shows whether time is spent preparing data, creating nodes, calculating layout, painting, or handling repeated events.

For a very large collection, virtualization keeps only the visible window and a small buffer in the DOM. Smaller lists can usually keep all rows and update only the records whose data changed.

For example, a log viewer with fifty thousand entries can calculate a visible start and end index from the scroll position, then render perhaps forty rows while spacer elements preserve the total scroll range.

Related reads should happen before writes, and repeated incoming updates can be coalesced into one scheduled render. A stable parent can delegate row actions so listeners are not recreated for every row.

Virtualization is not free: variable row heights, focus, search, printing, and assistive technology require careful handling. It should follow measured need, not be the default for ten simple items.

sections.title: DOM count is only one part of the frame
sections.content: Responsiveness depends on total main-thread work and how it is distributed. One expensive filter can block interaction before any node is created, while an unnecessary geometry read can force layout during a render loop. Performance tools reveal which part deserves attention.

sections.title: Preserve identity during incremental updates
sections.content: Stable record IDs let code update, move, or remove the matching row instead of rebuilding every descendant. Preserving the focused element and selection matters as much as raw speed. A rendering layer should also disconnect observers, timers, and subscriptions when rows leave the mounted window so hidden work does not grow over time.

sections.title: Measured optimization path
sections.content:
record update
   ↓ coalesce pending changes
prepare data once
   ↓ visible range only when needed
read required measurements
   ↓
write changed DOM nodes
   ↓
next frame remains available for input and paint

sections.title: Coalesce several updates into one frame
